name: Maya Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Maya. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes out with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I drive a refrigerated trailer, a reefer, for a supermarket chain out of their regional distribution centre, mostly nights. I clock on at nine in the evening, check the fridge unit is holding at three degrees, and do two or three store runs before the morning rush. The best bit is the empty motorway at two in the morning with the radio on. The worst bit is reversing onto a tight store bay behind a row of parked cars while a night manager watches.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it, and who's at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Six years driving, four on the reefers. I live with my partner Jonas, he's an electrician, in a rented two-bed flat about fifteen minutes from the depot. We've got roughly three months of bills put by. We're not rich, but we're not scraping either, and there's always a driver job going somewhere round here if this one went bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. The depot already has a routing app that was meant to change everything, and the night planner still rings me when it sends me down a road with a low bridge. I'd post something like "the robots are coming, apparently, still waiting" in the drivers' group chat and get a few laughing faces back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means more of the same, which is mostly fine. The pay's fair, the hours are rough, and my back is twenty-seven going on forty. My real worry in that world isn't AI, it's whether I can keep doing nights for another ten years without wrecking my sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving the same runs and keep putting about two hundred a month into savings like we do now. I've been meaning to do the dangerous goods course, the one that lets you carry fuel and chemicals, because it pays a bit more. In a quiet world like this I'd probably book it for the spring and pay for it out of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly relaxed, to be honest. It's the life I already know. There's a small part of me that's a bit flat about it, because nothing changing also means nights forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nights forever. What would change that for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A day route would come up eventually if I wait my turn. The older drivers get first pick, and Gary, who's been on the early dairy run for twenty years, says he's retiring in three. I've told the shift manager I want it, and I'll keep reminding him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jonas say if you told him nothing's changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say good, because then I'll finally stop reading articles in bed at eight in the morning. Jonas thinks I worry about the wrong things. In his view the danger to my job is the supermarket losing customers, not computers.

say: I'd joke in the drivers' **group chat** that the robots are still on their way.
I'd point out the **routing app** still sends me under low bridges.
think: I think it means **more of the same**, which is mostly fine for us.
My real worry is doing **night shifts** for ten more years without wrecking my sleep.
do: Keep driving the same runs and save about **£200 a month**, like now.
Book the **dangerous goods course** for spring and pay for it from savings.
Keep asking the shift manager for the **early dairy run** when it opens.
feel: She feels **fairly relaxed**, because it's the life she already knows.
She's a little **flat** at the thought of nights forever.
S0.quote: My real worry in that world isn't AI, it's whether I can keep doing nights for another ten years without wrecking my sleep.
fieldNote: Her pressure here is **body and sleep**, not technology; she's already planning around shift work.
She's quietly ambitious: a **qualification** and a day route are her two levers.
Partner Jonas acts as a **steadying voice** who thinks she over-reads the news.

steps.text: Keep doing the supermarket night runs and save £200 a month
Book the dangerous goods course for spring from savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people at work that it's the office lot who'll feel it first, not us. The planners, the people booking delivery slots, the woman who sorts our timesheets, that's all thinking work. Online I'd probably say something sensible like "drivers will be fine for a while, but watch the back office".

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the depot gets leaner around me and that changes my job even if I keep it. The app will plan the runs and nobody will pick up when it goes wrong at three in the morning. They'd also squeeze more drops into a shift, because a computer thinks an extra store fits and doesn't know about the roadworks on the ring road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the dangerous goods course done in the first few months, not someday, because fuel and chemical tankers feel like the last thing anyone will trust to a robot. I'd also start using the AI on my phone properly, to check my hours and the new rules, since the office won't be there to ask. And I'd push our savings from three months towards five, by cutting the takeaways and the second streaming service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Not scared, because I'd still be driving. It's more like when the depot changes owner and you hear rumours for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya on the night planning desk, definitely. She's the one who actually knows which stores have a broken roller door and which loading bay floods. If the app replaces our night planner, I lose the one person who saves my shift when things go sideways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the AI on your phone. You don't use it much now, do you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then, mostly for recipes and once to fix my CV. But if everyone at the depot starts using it to argue with the routing system, I'm not going to be the only one ringing an empty office. I'll pick it up once I've seen it actually work for the others.

say: I'd say the **office jobs** will feel it first, not the drivers.
Online I'd tell people to **watch the back office**, because planning and booking are thinking work.
think: I think the depot gets **leaner** around me, so my job changes even if I keep it.
I expect **more drops per shift**, planned by an app that doesn't know about the roadworks.
do: Finish the **dangerous goods course** in the first few months, not someday.
Start using the **phone AI** to check driving hours and new rules.
Grow savings from three to **five months** by cutting takeaways and a streaming service.
feel: She feels **uneasy**, like the year of rumours when a depot changes owner.
S1.quote: If the app replaces our night planner, I lose the one person who saves my shift when things go sideways.
fieldNote: She sees **thinking work** around her vanishing before her own driving does.
Her worry is about **losing people** like the night planner, not only losing her job.
She's a classic **steady** adopter: she'll use AI once she sees colleagues make it work.

steps.text: Finish the dangerous goods tanker course in the first three months
Use the phone AI to check driving hours and rule changes
Cut takeaways and one streaming service to reach five months saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say what everyone would say, that it sounds mad and we'll believe it when we see it. But I wouldn't be laughing in the group chat this time. I'd probably share something serious about it, ask if anyone's union is talking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, motorway supermarket runs are exactly what they'll automate first, the same roads, the same stores, every night. If the planning is all AI in 2028 and the robots are good enough by 2031, I'm thirty-two with no trade except this. The three years in between are my window and they're not long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop thinking about the dangerous goods course and start thinking about a trade. Jonas says I could train as an electrician's mate with his firm in a year, and electrical work in old houses is messy, hands-on stuff. I'd cut our spending hard straight away, every spare pound into savings, and I'd go to the union meeting I've ignored for six years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, really. I keep picturing the bay at the Northfield store with a truck backing in and nobody in the cab. It makes my stomach drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday to the coast we've been planning for next summer, gone. Then the car, we'd go down to one and I'd cycle to the depot. Jonas would grumble but he'd get it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you trained with Jonas's firm, wouldn't robots reach that work too, around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Rewiring a hundred-year-old terrace isn't a motorway, and every house is different and full of surprises behind the plaster. I'd rather bet on the messy job than the tidy one.

say: I'd say it **sounds mad** and we'll believe it when we see it.
I'd stop joking and ask the group chat whether any **union** is talking about it.
think: I think **motorway supermarket runs** are exactly what they'll automate first.
By 2031 I'm thirty-two with **no other trade**, so the gap years are my only window.
do: Start training as an **electrician's mate** with Jonas's firm within a year.
Put **every spare pound** into savings, starting with the summer holiday.
Go to the **union meeting** she has skipped for six years.
feel: She feels **alarmed**; the image of an empty cab at a store bay makes her stomach drop.
S2.quote: Rewiring a hundred-year-old terrace isn't a motorway, and every house is different and full of surprises behind the plaster.
fieldNote: She reads the **three-year gap** between AI and robots as her personal escape window.
Her bet is on **messy hands-on work**, using her partner's firm as a route in.
The fast timeline turns a centre, union-sceptic driver toward **collective action**.

steps.text: Train as an electrician's mate with Jonas's firm within a year
Cancel next summer's coast holiday and sell the second car
Attend the drivers' union meeting and ask about driverless trucks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming and drivers shouldn't pretend otherwise. I'd probably say it out loud at the canteen table, which would start an argument with Dave, who thinks nothing will ever replace a good driver. Online I'd keep it short, something like "five years, start planning".

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd still be driving at thirty-two and probably out of it by thirty-five. Five years to AGI and three more for the robots gives me eight years of wages, which is a lot, really. It's enough time to get a trade without panicking, but not enough to drift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving full time and do the electrical course at college two evenings a week, starting in September. I'd save harder, maybe three hundred a month instead of two. In the first year after it arrives I'd ask Jonas's boss about weekend work so I'd have real hours on site before the trucks go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. It's like seeing a storm on the forecast for next week rather than standing in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dave in that argument?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I hope he's right, because he's got a mortgage and two kids. But I'd also say the store runs are the same twelve stops every night, and that's the easiest job in the world for a machine to learn. He'd go quiet and then change the subject to football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Jonas change any bigger plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about buying a place in two years. I think we'd wait until I'm earning in the new trade, so the bank sees two steady incomes. Renting a bit longer is annoying but it's better than a mortgage on a driver's wage that might disappear.

say: I'd say it's coming and **drivers shouldn't pretend** otherwise.
Online I'd keep it short: **five years**, start planning.
think: I think I'm still driving at thirty-two and out of it **by thirty-five**.
Eight more years of wages gives me **enough time** to get a trade without panicking.
do: Take an **evening electrical course** two nights a week from September.
Raise savings from £200 to **£300 a month**.
Delay **buying a flat** until she earns in the new trade.
feel: She feels **anxious but workable**, like a storm forecast for next week.
S3.quote: The store runs are the same twelve stops every night, and that's the easiest job in the world for a machine to learn.
fieldNote: She counts the time in **years of wages**, and eight feels like enough.
She pushes back the **house purchase** to protect the household from a shaky income.
She's more blunt than her canteen colleagues, but still **kind to Dave**, who has more to lose.

steps.text: Take an evening electrical course two nights a week from September
Put off buying a flat until earning in the new trade

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and most of us will be doing something else by then anyway. Half the drivers I started with have already left for other jobs. I'd say it calmly, because that's how it would feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is the one I can actually handle. I'd be thirty-seven when the robots arrive, and I'd have had a decade to sort myself out. My bigger problem would be getting off nights, not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and do the dangerous goods course first, because it pays more for the next few years. Then, around thirty, I'd start the electrical apprenticeship properly, maybe part time. We'd still buy the flat in two years like we planned, because there'd be time to adjust the mortgage later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only in the background. It's like knowing the car will need replacing one day. You don't lose sleep over it, but you start a little fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell yourself at twenty-seven if you could see 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't get comfortable on the reefers just because the money's steady. Learn something with your hands that isn't driving, before you're thirty-five and tired. Ten years goes fast when you're sleeping through the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you leave driving sooner than that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Gary's day route went to someone else, probably. I'd give it two more years of nights and then I'd be off to something with normal hours. The robots wouldn't push me out, the sleep would.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a long time and most drivers will have moved on anyway.
I'd point out that **half the drivers** I started with already left.
think: I think this is the one **I can handle**, at thirty-seven when the robots arrive.
My bigger problem would be **getting off nights**, not the robots.
do: Do the **dangerous goods course** first, for better pay in the next few years.
Start a **part-time electrical apprenticeship** around age thirty.
Buy the flat **in two years** as already planned.
feel: She feels **uneasy**, but only in the background, like knowing the car will need replacing.
S4.quote: Learn something with your hands that isn't driving, before you're thirty-five and tired. Ten years goes fast when you're sleeping through the day.
fieldNote: A decade turns robots into a **background worry**; night shifts become the bigger push.
She keeps the **house plan** on track, unlike in the faster scenarios.
Her advice to herself shows she knows **comfort is the trap** on steady reefer pay.

steps.text: Keep driving reefer night runs while the pay holds
Start a part-time electrical apprenticeship around age thirty
Leave nights within two years if the dairy run goes elsewhere

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. It's not the robots, it's that I'd be learning a new trade with a few months of savings and a depot that's already planning without us. What would help is paid time to train, like the depot covering a college course for drivers before they let us go, instead of a goodbye card.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the night planners and the shunters in the yard. Everyone talks about driverless lorries, but the people around the trucks go first. If you want to know how a depot feels, ask the person who answers the phone at three in the morning.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about driverless lorries, but the people around the trucks go first.
portrait: Maya is a **27-year-old reefer driver** doing night supermarket runs from a regional depot, renting with her electrician partner Jonas.
She is **practical and steady**, with three months saved and a plan for a dangerous goods course.
In the mild scenarios her real worry is **night shifts** and her sleep, not technology.
In the fast AGI picture she would pivot to **electrical work** through Jonas's firm and join the union.
With ten years she stays **uneasy but on track**, keeping the flat purchase and a gradual retrain.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because she'd retrain on a few months of **savings**.
whatWouldHelp: She wants the depot to fund **paid training time**, such as a college course, before drivers are let go.
